slides.text: When I moved to a coastal Scottish village to clear out my grandmother's estate, I swore off romance forever. Then I met Arthur. He was the local carpenter—built like a mountain, with hands rougher than tree bark, and infuriatingly silent. I was an anxious American writer who rambled constantly. We made no sense. Yet, he fixed my roof, chopped my firewood, and left wild heather on my porch. But he never actually said a single word about his feelings.

Frustrated by his silence, I packed my bags to leave. On my final evening, he knocked on my door. He stood in the freezing rain, soaking wet, clutching a massive, leather-bound Gaelic dictionary. He shoved it into my hands without making eye contact. 'Page two-hundred-and-forty,' he rumbled, his thick Scottish accent heavy and desperate. 'Third word down. I don't know how to say it in English without sounding like a fool. Just... read it before you go.'

I slammed the door and flipped through the yellowed pages, my hands trembling. Page 240. Third word down. Mo-chreach. The literal translation was 'my ruin' or 'my destruction.' But the dictionary's faded margins had a handwritten note, scrawled in Arthur's messy handwriting: 'Used when someone loves another person so intensely that it completely undoes them. You are my ruin, Elara. Stay.' I dropped the heavy book, threw open the front door, and ran straight into his waiting arms.
